column5: watering furrows; soil softened for grain
column6: The commentary begins with rain squeezed from clouds and later with crops; this psalm has God water the furrows and prepare grain, joining rainfall directly to yield.

column5: early rain and latter rain
column6: The commentary links rain to plants that grow after it; Joel's restoration promise names seasonal rains as the setting for renewed agricultural abundance.

column5: threshing floor full
column6: After Joel's rain promise, this verse says the threshing floors fill with grain and vats overflow, giving the same rain-to-harvest sequence the commentary draws from cloud to crop.

column5: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
column6: The commentary moves from rain to plant growth and harvest; Isaiah's rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts, supplying seed for sowing and bread for food, a closely matched growth sequence.

column5: grass for cattle; plants for people
column6: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and describes grain as human yield; this verse pairs God-grown grass for cattle with plants for human use.

column5: pastures with flocks; valleys with grain
column6: The commentary connects rain-fed pasture and harvested grain; this verse places flocks in pasture and grain in valleys in one picture of a fruitful landscape.

column5: fat cows grazing beside lean cows
column6: The commentary's camel fattens on spring growth; Pharaoh's dream makes fat, grazing cows the sign of abundant years, with their lean counterparts marking the coming reversal.

column5: green pasture and still waters
column6: The commentary describes pasture nourishing a herd; the shepherd here leads the speaker to green pasture and water, adding a personal image of provision that prevents want.

column5: tree beside water; fruit in season
column6: The commentary pictures the exception to loss as plants joined in unbroken greenery; Psalm 1's planted tree bears fruit at its time and its leaf does not wither, giving that flourishing a righteous figure.

column5: chaff driven by wind
column6: The commentary's whirlwind lifts dust and its crop image ends in disappearance; Psalm 1 contrasts its fruiting tree with the wicked as wind-scattered chaff.

column5: watered tree endures heat and drought
column6: The commentary's connected greenery stands against the lost harvest; Jeremiah's tree by water stays green in heat and continues bearing fruit even in drought, a specific image of endurance.

column5: fruit in old age; fresh and green
column6: The commentary says a life's accumulated crop can be lost in its late years; this psalm instead says the righteous still bear fruit in old age, explicitly reversing that late-life outcome.

column5: עצר; rain restrained (table sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary's ع ص ر image releases rain from a pressed cloud; the package's table gives Hebrew עצר as a sound correspondence, and this verse uses it for heaven being restrained so rain and land-yield cease.

column5: חשר; collection of watery clouds (table notes BDB's Arabic cognate)
column6: The commentary develops rain-bearing and layered clouds, while the package's חשר entry describes a gathering of watery clouds and notes an Arabic cognate; Job's context concerns the spread of clouds, so the lexical link is suggestive but uncertain.

column5: חסר; lack (table sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary labels خسر as the loss of a harvest; the package lists חסר as a corresponding Hebrew root, and the shepherd-speaker says he will not lack, giving a concrete opposite outcome under care.

column5: מחסור; lack of everything (table sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary glosses خسر as a crop's disappearance; the package's חסר correspondence appears here in a covenant curse of hunger, thirst, nakedness, and total lack, making the loss material and collective.

column5: צבר; grain heaped up (table sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary gives صبرة as food piled upon food; the package lists צבר as a sound correspondence, and Genesis uses it for Joseph's immense heaping of grain, matching the concrete heap sense.

column5: חק; a prescribed share of produce (table sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary calls the crop's due on harvest day its حق; the package's חקק correspondence means something prescribed, and Genesis fixes a fifth of the land's yield as a statute, making the crop's allotted share concrete.

column5: forgotten sheaf left for the vulnerable
column6: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; this law leaves a forgotten sheaf for the immigrant, orphan, and widow, showing harvested produce as a social obligation.

column5: sowing much, gathering little to locusts
column6: The commentary's central loss image is a vanished harvest; this curse has abundant sowing yield little because locusts consume it, specifying one way the crop is lost.

column5: produce worked for but not enjoyed
column6: The commentary says a lifetime's yield can disappear; Micah names sowing without reaping, olives without oil, and grapes without wine, turning that loss into denied agricultural labor.

column5: sow righteousness; reap steadfast love; rain righteousness
column6: The commentary joins good deeds and mutual counsel to its green-growth image; Hosea commands sowing righteousness and seeking God until rain comes, linking ethical action to a promised harvest.

column5: sowing in tears, reaping in joy
column6: The commentary pairs steadfastness with the crop's rise and loss; this psalm makes a painful sowing issue in joyful reaping, adding a hope-filled harvest after hardship.

column5: sow morning and evening without slackening
column6: The commentary's exception holds to patient good work; Ecclesiastes tells the sower not to rest because the successful yield is unknown, giving patience an agricultural practice.

column5: grass and flower wither when wind blows
column6: The commentary's cyclone lifts dust and destroys the crop; Isaiah says grass withers when the divine breath blows and identifies people with grass, bringing human transience into the weather image.

column5: tumbleweed and chaff before wind
column6: The commentary describes a whirlwind lifting dust into a column; this verse makes enemies like rolling dust and wind-driven chaff, using airborne scattering as an image of defeat.

column5: fire consuming forest
column6: The commentary's fiery cyclone burns a garden; this verse compares judgment on enemies to fire consuming a forest, extending the storm image to vegetation destroyed by flame.

column5: storm and tempest pursuing enemies
column6: The commentary's إعصار is a destructive wind column; this verse calls for enemies to be pursued by storm and tempest, using violent weather as an image of reversal and judgment.

column5: continue the work without needing to finish it
column6: The commentary's righteous community keeps urging patience while doing good; this maxim says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence when a lifetime may not see the yield.

column5: stalk, head, then full grain
column6: The commentary says the grain is named عصر when its husk appears and then describes its yield; Mark's seed parable traces growth through stalk, head, and full grain, closely matching that crop-stage sequence.

column5: sickle when the harvest is ready
column6: The commentary moves from grain's formation to its yield; Mark ends the growing sequence with the sickle at harvest, supplying the moment when the crop becomes gathered produce.

column5: fruit borne with endurance
column6: The commentary joins good deeds and patience to its crop imagery; Luke's good-soil hearers hold fast and bear fruit with endurance, directly linking ethical reception to patient yield.

column5: farmer waits for fruit and early and late rain
column6: The commentary connects rain-fed growth with patience; James tells believers to wait like a farmer for the earth's precious fruit through the rains, adding patient expectation to the crop image.

column5: community told to be patient and strengthen hearts
column6: The commentary says the righteous mutually urge one another to patience; James addresses the community and tells them to be patient and steady-hearted as the Lord's coming draws near.

column5: doing good reaped in due season
column6: The commentary links righteous action and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because the harvest comes at its season if they do not give up, making the ethical crop analogy explicit.

column5: rained land produces useful vegetation
column6: The commentary's cloud gives rain and the exception is a green, productive community; Hebrews compares hearers to land that drinks frequent rain and produces useful vegetation, interpreting response as fruitful growth.

column5: thorns, curse, and burning
column6: The commentary's storm can burn an entire garden; Hebrews contrasts productive land with ground bearing thorns and thistles, near a curse and destined for burning.

column5: vine and branches bear fruit by remaining joined
column6: The commentary says those excepted from loss interconnect like continuous greenery; Jesus depicts branches joined to a vine and bearing much fruit by abiding, giving the joined-plant image a communal source of fruitfulness.

column5: severed branch withers and is burned
column6: The commentary's crop can be destroyed by a fiery whirlwind; Jesus says the branch that does not abide withers, is gathered, and burned, joining disconnection, loss, and fire.

column5: truth spoken as the body grows
column6: The commentary's people mutually counsel one another to truth; Ephesians joins speaking truth with growing into Christ, adding growth as the outcome of truthful communal practice.

column5: joined body grows as each part works
column6: The commentary makes mutual counsel into plants connected as one green pasture; Ephesians describes a body joined together with every part working so it grows and builds itself up, a specific social counterpart to interconnected growth.

column5: admonish, encourage, help, and be patient with all
column6: The commentary's exception consists of people who urge one another to truth and patience; Paul specifies communal admonition, encouragement of the fainthearted, help for the weak, and patience toward all.

column5: rain and wind strike a house founded on rock, but it stands
column6: The commentary pairs a destructive storm with hard stone; Jesus' house withstands rain, flood, and wind because it is founded on rock, making stability the opposite outcome of the ruined garden.

column5: grain dies and bears much fruit
column6: The commentary's late-life storm destroys a life's yield; Jesus says a grain of wheat that dies produces much fruit, turning the death of a seed into multiplication rather than loss.

column5: work burned and its maker suffers loss, yet is saved
column6: The commentary likens failed works to ash blown away; Paul says a person's work may be burned and suffer loss while the person is saved, distinguishing lost product from lost person.

column5: abundant crops stored in larger barns
column6: The commentary's harvest can represent a life's accumulated product; the rich man plans larger barns for his abundant produce, making stored yield the object later put at risk.

column5: life required before stored goods can be used
column6: The commentary says the storm may destroy the whole accumulation late in life; the rich man is told that his life is required that night and is asked who will own his stored goods, making the harvest's futility personal.

column5: water bound in clouds; cloud holds its burden
column6: The commentary's cloud is compressed with rain before releasing it; Job depicts God binding water in clouds without their bursting, adding a precise image of cloud containment.

column5: small cloud rising from the sea
column6: The commentary develops rain-bearing clouds; Elijah's servant sees a cloud rising from the sea, a specific cloud sign that precedes the rain.

column5: sky blackens and heavy rain begins
column6: The commentary moves from a rain cloud to the water it releases; after the small cloud, this verse describes darkening skies and heavy rain, completing that weather sequence.

column5: rain sent where no person lives
column6: The commentary pictures rain delivered to a community; Job asks about rain given to an uninhabited land, adding the counterpoint that rain also serves places without human recipients.

column5: wilderness satisfied; grass sprouts
column6: The commentary links rain with greening plants; Job's next verse says the desolate land is satisfied and tender grass sprouts, spelling out the water-to-growth result.

column5: storm clouds, showers, and field grass
column6: The commentary links a rain cloud to pasture growth; Zechariah asks for rain from the maker of storm clouds, which gives showers and field grass.

column5: riverside trees fruit every month; leaves do not wither
column6: The commentary's exception is continuous interconnected greenery; Ezekiel's riverbank trees never fail to fruit and keep healing leaves, extending the image to perennial abundance.

column5: feed the hungry and satisfy the afflicted
column6: The commentary assigns the harvest a due and makes righteous action part of its green community; Isaiah makes feeding the hungry the condition of the promised light and renewal that follows.

column5: watered garden and unfailing spring
column6: The commentary joins righteous practice to a rain-fed green world; Isaiah promises that the person who acts for the hungry will be like a watered garden whose spring does not fail.

column5: honor God with firstfruits
column6: The commentary says the crop has a due on harvest day; Proverbs gives the first produce to honor God, making the yield a prescribed offering.

column5: full barns and overflowing vats
column6: The commentary traces rain through crop to gathered produce; Proverbs depicts full barns and overflowing wine vats as the result of honoring God with firstfruits.

column5: first produce placed in a basket
column6: The commentary names the crop's due on harvest day; Deuteronomy requires the first of the land's produce to be gathered in a basket, giving that due a ritual form.

column5: firstfruits presented before God
column6: The commentary connects harvest to an owed share; this verse has the worshipper present the firstfruits as an offering, making the harvest's claim a liturgical act.

column5: rejoice with Levite and immigrant
column6: The commentary makes fruitful life a shared community image; the firstfruits rite culminates in rejoicing with the Levite and immigrant, extending the crop's benefit beyond its grower.

column5: threshing ox allowed to eat grain
column6: The commentary says pasture gives itself to the herd and the harvest has a due; this law lets the working ox eat from the grain it threshes, assigning a share of produce to the animal laborer.

column5: עצר; festival assembly (table's sound correspondence only)
column6: The commentary describes rain falling on a community; the package's table pairs Arabic ع ص ر with Hebrew עצר and lists festival assembly as a Hebrew use, while Leviticus names an assembly at the ingathering festival. This is a lexical and communal echo, not proof of cognacy.

column5: sowing wind, reaping whirlwind; stalk without a head yields no flour
column6: The commentary's cyclone raises dust and its lost harvest disappears; Hosea binds whirlwind to failed grain, explicitly saying the stalk has no head and yields no flour.

column5: great wind collapses a house and kills the children inside
column6: The commentary's fiery storm destroys a garden while its owner has weak children; Job's wind destroys a household and its children, adding the family cost of a sudden storm, though the objects and cause differ.

column5: flour and oil do not run out during drought
column6: The commentary presents the harvest as lost; during a drought, the widow's flour and oil remain sufficient, a specific counterexample of provision continuing without a new crop.

column5: sowing to flesh reaps corruption; sowing to Spirit reaps life
column6: The commentary says humanity is in loss except those who do good; Paul assigns contrasting harvests to two ways of life, making the ethical distinction a direct sowing-and-reaping contrast.

column5: seed scattered on the ground
column6: The commentary follows rain through plant growth to harvest; Jesus begins a kingdom parable with a person scattering seed, adding the human act that starts the growth sequence.

column5: seed grows while the sower does not know how
column6: The commentary makes the rain-fed growth of plants an image for a community's flourishing; in Jesus' parable the earth produces growth beyond the sower's understanding, adding the hidden process between sowing and harvest.

column5: one plants, another waters, God gives growth
column6: The commentary turns plants joined together into people who urge one another; Paul describes distinct workers planting and watering within one field, while God supplies the growth.

column5: generous sowing yields a generous harvest
column6: The commentary links righteous deeds and harvest; Paul applies sowing and reaping to generosity, making shared giving the deed that determines the yield.

column5: seed for sowing and a growing harvest of righteousness
column6: The commentary joins good works to a crop image; Paul says God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness, explicitly making ethical fruit the result.

column5: plowman and thresher hope to share the crop
column6: The commentary says produce has a due and pasture nourishes animals; Paul interprets the crop law as giving field workers hope of sharing the harvest, making labor and entitlement explicit.

column5: reaper gathers fruit for life and sower and reaper rejoice together
column6: The commentary pictures a community made fruitful through linked action; Jesus describes harvest workers rejoicing together as fruit is gathered, giving shared labor and shared outcome a concrete scene.

column5: one sows while another reaps
column6: The commentary connects mutual exhortation with plants joined into continuous growth; Jesus' saying assigns sowing and reaping to different people, making cooperation across roles explicit.

column5: reaping what others labored to sow
column6: The commentary's green community is formed through reciprocal action; Jesus says his hearers enter work others began, adding continuity across generations of sowers and reapers.

column5: fig tree given another year and extra care
column6: The commentary joins patience to the crop's fate; the gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize a fruitless fig tree, making patience an intervention that could change the harvest.

column5: fruit determines whether the tree is spared or cut down
column6: The commentary contrasts productive greenery with crop loss; the gardener's final condition is that the tree bear fruit or be cut down, making the outcome hinge on yield.

column5: weeds burned while wheat is gathered
column6: The commentary distinguishes the fruitful exception from a lost harvest; Jesus' harvest separates wheat for storage from weeds for burning, adding a final sorting of productive and useless growth.

column5: rain falls on just and unjust alike
column6: The commentary's cloud releases rain onto a community while its later image distinguishes the righteous exception; Jesus says rain falls on both just and unjust, adding an account of weather as an indiscriminate gift.

column5: hail and fire burn trees and green grass
column6: The commentary's fire-bearing whirlwind burns a garden; Revelation's first trumpet sends hail and fire onto the earth, burning trees and green grass in an apocalyptic destruction scene.

column5: one person sharpens another
column6: The commentary interprets connected plants as people who counsel one another; Proverbs gives mutual sharpening as a concrete image of how one person forms another, though it does not use agricultural imagery.

column5: good deeds have fruit in this world and a principal kept for the next
column6: The commentary exempts people who believe, do good, and counsel one another; Peah lists kindness and peacemaking among deeds whose fruit is enjoyed now while their principal remains for the world to come, giving the ethical exception a rabbinic account of reward.
